method_note: Primary Arabic used where present (Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Qurtubi, Saadi). Jalalayn and attrib. Ibn Abbas are English-only in the live tafsir_entries dataset; that absence is preserved rather than silently substituted.

propositions.statement_en: Al-Tabari identifies 'Our Spirit' in 19:17 as Gabriel.
Ibn Kathir identifies 'Our Spirit' in 19:17 as Gabriel and says this identification is the apparent sense of the Qur'an.
A report from Ubayy ibn Ka'b says the spirit that appeared to Mary was the spirit of Jesus; Ibn Kathir rejects this as extremely strange, objectionable, and apparently Israelite material.
Al-Qurtubi records an unnamed view that 'Our Spirit' is the spirit of Jesus, created before bodies and placed into Jesus in Mary's womb.
Al-Qurtubi says the apparent interpretation is that 'Our Spirit' is Gabriel, because the following clause describes the angel assuming human form.
Al-Sa'di identifies 'Our Spirit' in 19:17 as Gabriel.
Jalalayn identifies 'Our Spirit' in 19:17 as Gabriel, who appeared as a well-proportioned human.
The attributed Ibn Abbas entry identifies 'Our Spirit' in 19:17 as God's messenger Gabriel.
Al-Tabari identifies the speaker who tells Mary 'I am only a messenger of your Lord' as 'Our Spirit,' i.e. Gabriel.
Al-Qurtubi explicitly identifies the speaker of 19:19 as Gabriel.
Al-Sa'di explicitly identifies the speaker of 19:19 as Gabriel, carrying out his Lord's message concerning Mary.

Al-Tabari prefers the reading la-ahaba ('that I may give you') in 19:19, understanding the messenger to say he was sent to give Mary the pure boy, and rejects departing from the communal codices and dominant reading.
Al-Qurtubi explains la-ahaba ('that I may give') as attributing the gift to Gabriel because the announcement came through him, while the reading li-yahaba makes Allah the giver.
Ibn Kathir says both readings of 19:19, la-ahaba and li-yahaba, have a sound interpretation and each entails the other.
Al-Tabari glosses the 'pure' boy (ghulaman zakiyyan) as one purified from sins.
Al-Sa'di interprets the boy's purity as purification from blameworthy traits together with possession of praiseworthy traits.
Jalalayn glosses the boy as pure in his prophethood.

Al-Qurtubi interprets 'no man has touched me' as absence of marital intercourse and 'I have not been unchaste' as denial of fornication, making the latter an emphatic exclusion of unlawful intercourse.
Al-Tabari interprets Mary's statement as excluding both lawful intercourse through marriage and unlawful intercourse through fornication.
Al-Qurtubi says Mary was not doubting God's power; she was asking by what mechanism the child would come—through a future husband or by direct divine creation.
Al-Tabari understands Mary to ask whether she would obtain a son through a husband she would marry or whether God would initiate his creation directly in her.

Ibn Kathir presents Jesus' fatherless birth as completing four modes of human creation—Adam without male or female, Eve from male without female, ordinary offspring from male and female, and Jesus from female without male—demonstrating God's perfect power.

Al-Sa'di says Jesus' miraculous birth demonstrates that created causes have no independent efficacy; God sometimes breaks customary causal patterns so people do not mistake causes for their Determiner.
Al-Qurtubi interprets Jesus as a sign in the sense of a wondrous proof of God's power.
Al-Tabari interprets Jesus as a sign and proof to God's creation and as a mercy to Mary and to those who believe in and affirm him.

Al-Sa'di explains the mercy of Jesus in three directions: mercy to Jesus through revelation and prophetic rank, mercy to Mary through honor and benefit, and mercy to people through a messenger whose teaching and obedience lead to well-being in this life and the next.
Ibn Kathir interprets 'a mercy from Us' as Jesus being made a prophet who calls people to worship Allah and affirm His oneness.
Jalalayn reconstructs the conception as Gabriel breathing into the opening of Mary's shirt by God's command, after which she sensed the formed fetus in her womb.

Ibn Kathir gives two possibilities for 'it was a matter decreed': it may continue Gabriel's speech to Mary about a matter fixed in God's knowledge, decree, and will, or it may be God's report to Muhammad connected with the breathing into Mary.

evidence_units.content_summary: Qatadah identifies 'Our Spirit' in 19:17 as Gabriel in al-Tabari.
Wahb ibn Munabbih reports that Gabriel appeared to Mary as a well-proportioned human in al-Tabari.

Muhammad ibn Sahl -> Isma'il ibn Abd al-Karim -> Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil -> Wahb ibn Munabbih

evidence_units.content_summary: Ibn Jurayj identifies 'Our Spirit' in 19:17 as Gabriel in al-Tabari.
Ubayy ibn Ka'b report preserved by Ibn Kathir identifies the appearing spirit as the spirit of Jesus; Ibn Kathir rejects the report.

routes.route_description: Abu Ja'far al-Razi -> al-Rabi' ibn Anas -> Abu al-Aliya -> Ubayy ibn Ka'b

evidence_links.semantic_link_note: One of al-Tabari's named-source reports supporting his Gabriel identification.
Wahb's report independently describes Gabriel as the human-form visitor in al-Tabari, with two preserved routes.
A further named-source report in al-Tabari explicitly identifying the Spirit as Gabriel.
The Ubayy report is the source of the Jesus-spirit alternative that Ibn Kathir explicitly rejects.
